questions.q: What definition of wisdom does the editorial give?
options: The ability to discover the relevant by sorting out the irrelevant
Yes. Clarity of thought follows from it.
The experience that comes with age
Not quite. The article says: The ability to discover the relevant by sorting out the irrelevant.
The ability to speak well
Not quite. The article says: The ability to discover the relevant by sorting out the irrelevant.
The possession of much information
Not quite. The article says: The ability to discover the relevant by sorting out the irrelevant.
questions.rationale: “Wisdom is the ability to discover the relevant by sorting out the irrelevant.”

questions.q: In early Makkah the Kabah was in the hands of those who opposed the Prophet’s message. How does the editorial describe his response?
options: He demanded control of it first
Not quite. The article says: He did not react; he saw the people gathered there as an audience and used the opportunity to convey his message.
He did not react; he saw the people gathered there as an audience and used the opportunity to convey his message
Well read. Avoid the unwanted; plan on what is available.
He waited until the gatherings ended
Not quite. The article says: He did not react; he saw the people gathered there as an audience and used the opportunity to convey his message.
He stayed away from the Kabah altogether
Not quite. The article says: He did not react; he saw the people gathered there as an audience and used the opportunity to convey his message.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet of Islam never reacted to this situation. He studied the situation and found that this assembly was a potential audience for his message.”

questions.q: When the Prophet returned shaken from the cave of Hira, how did Khadija help him?
options: She reassured him that no harm would come to one so truthful and kind to others
Right. Gentleness and understanding calmed him.
She advised him to tell no one
Not quite. The article says: She reassured him that no harm would come to one so truthful and kind to others.
She asked him to return to the cave
Not quite. The article says: She reassured him that no harm would come to one so truthful and kind to others.
She sent for the elders of the town
Not quite. The article says: She reassured him that no harm would come to one so truthful and kind to others.
questions.rationale: “She did her best to assure him that no harm would come to him as he always spoke the truth, helped the poor and those in distress, and invariably treated others with respect.”

questions.q: The emperor Akbar, insulted in court by his teacher, wished to punish him. What did his mother, Maryam Makani, tell him?
options: That history would remember an emperor with all power who forgave
Yes. She calmed him and the man was spared.
That an emperor must never be insulted
Not quite. The article says: That history would remember an emperor with all power who forgave.
That the court should decide
Not quite. The article says: That history would remember an emperor with all power who forgave.
That the teacher should be sent away
Not quite. The article says: That history would remember an emperor with all power who forgave.
questions.rationale: “She told him that his pardon would go down in history; that history would remember that ‘an emperor, having all the power at his disposal, forgave an offender’.”

questions.q: You choose to walk, yet you need the earth, gravity and air to do so. What does this example show about freedom and destiny?
options: Man has no freedom at all
Not quite. The article says: Man is free in his will, but can act only within an “infrastructure” set by the Creator.
Man is free in his will, but can act only within an “infrastructure” set by the Creator
Well reasoned. A balance between the two.
Freedom belongs only to the strong
Not quite. The article says: Man is free in his will, but can act only within an “infrastructure” set by the Creator.
Man is free of every limit
Not quite. The article says: Man is free in his will, but can act only within an “infrastructure” set by the Creator.
questions.rationale: “In terms of using his will, he is completely free. But he is helpless in the sense that he cannot use his free will without the infrastructure that has been established by the Creator.”

questions.q: When the Prophet Solomon received a blessing, what did he say?
options: “This is by the grace of my Lord”
Correct. Gratitude is acknowledging the real Giver.
“This is my inheritance”
Not quite. The article says: “This is by the grace of my Lord”.
“This is the gift of my people”
Not quite. The article says: “This is by the grace of my Lord”.
“This is the fruit of my effort”
Not quite. The article says: “This is by the grace of my Lord”.
questions.rationale: “When the Prophet Solomon received a worldly blessing he immediately said: Haza min fazli rabbi, which means, ‘This is by the grace of my Lord.’ (27: 40)”

questions.q: The article recalls Charlie Chaplin, who made the world laugh yet was unhappy within. What does it conclude about this world?
options: Happiness comes from laughing more
Not quite. The article says: It is made for action; lasting happiness belongs to the Hereafter.
Comedians are sadder than other people
Not quite. The article says: It is made for action; lasting happiness belongs to the Hereafter.
Happiness depends on fame
Not quite. The article says: It is made for action; lasting happiness belongs to the Hereafter.
It is made for action; lasting happiness belongs to the Hereafter
Yes. Here one can only work towards it.
questions.rationale: “The Creator has created the present world for action. Here only action to achieve happiness is possible and not happiness per se.”

questions.q: Ritual without spirit is “like a nutshell without a kernel.” What value does the article still see in it?
options: It replaces the need for spirit
Not quite. The article says: It keeps religion in mind and serves as a regular reminder of the spirit.
It keeps religion in mind and serves as a regular reminder of the spirit
Right. Form symbolises the inner content.
None at all
Not quite. The article says: It keeps religion in mind and serves as a regular reminder of the spirit.
It is equal to ritual with spirit
Not quite. The article says: It keeps religion in mind and serves as a regular reminder of the spirit.
questions.rationale: “This minimum role of rituals can be described as a reminder of spirit through routine.”

questions.q: Man alone has a sense of “tomorrow” and dies with ambitions unfulfilled. What does the article infer from this?
options: That life should be made longer
Not quite. The article says: That another world must follow in which human hopes, and justice, find fulfilment.
That animals are happier than man
Not quite. The article says: That another world must follow in which human hopes, and justice, find fulfilment.
That another world must follow in which human hopes, and justice, find fulfilment
Well read. Otherwise man alone would be left incomplete.
That man should have fewer ambitions
Not quite. The article says: That another world must follow in which human hopes, and justice, find fulfilment.
questions.rationale: “This indicates that there is a world that will come after this present one, a world where human beings will find complete fulfilment of their wishes and hopes.”

questions.q: Why, according to the commentary, was belief declared only after seeing the punishment of no avail?
options: Because it came from the wealthy
Not quite. The article says: Acceptance of truth has value when reached through reason, not when forced by what is seen.
Acceptance of truth has value when reached through reason, not when forced by what is seen
Exactly. The test is to recognise truth by its arguments.
Because it was spoken too softly
Not quite. The article says: Acceptance of truth has value when reached through reason, not when forced by what is seen.
Because too many people declared it together
Not quite. The article says: Acceptance of truth has value when reached through reason, not when forced by what is seen.
questions.rationale: “Only that admission of truth is desirable and useful which is arrived at on the basis of arguments.”
